title: Name That Growth
blurb: Most complexities come from a recognizable code shape. Match each Big-O to the pattern that usually produces it — this is the mental shortcut you use in interviews.

levels.title: L1 · The everyday shapes
levels.prompt: Match each complexity to the code pattern that causes it.
levels.hint: For each pattern ask: how many elements does it touch, and how many times?

right.label: a hash-map / array lookup, or fixed arithmetic
halving the search range each step (binary search)
a single pass over the input
nested loops over the same input

levels.explain: The mental shortcut: constant work → O(1); halving the range each step → O(log n); one full pass → O(n); nested loops over the same data → O(n²).

failStates.title: A single pass is O(n), not O(1)
failStates.explain: Touching every element once scales with n → O(n). O(1) is when the work is fixed no matter how big the input is — like one dictionary lookup.

failStates.title: O(log n) never touches most elements
failStates.explain: A full pass is O(n). O(log n) means you discard a fraction each step (like binary search) and only ever look at ~log n elements.

levels.title: L2 · Add sorting and brute force
levels.prompt: Two more shapes worth recognizing on sight.
levels.hint: Which pattern divides-and-conquers (a log factor), and which explores every combination?

right.label: sorting the input, then a linear pass
trying every subset / naive recursive branching
a single pass over the input
nested loops over the same input

levels.explain: Sorting-then-scanning is O(n log n) because the sort dominates; trying every subset or branching recursively is O(2ⁿ). A single pass stays O(n) and nesting stays O(n²).

failStates.title: Sorting is O(n log n), not O(n²)
failStates.explain: A good sort (merge/quick) is O(n log n). O(n²) comes from nested loops over the same data — a different shape entirely.

failStates.title: Nested loops give O(n²)
failStates.explain: Two nested passes over the same input multiply → n × n = O(n²). The log factor in O(n log n) comes from divide-and-conquer (like sorting), not nesting.
